title: The EU AI Act and Financial Services (EU Edition)
summary: An eight-module programme on the EU AI Act for supervisors and financial firms: risk classification, high-risk credit and insurance uses, provider and deployer duties, supervision and compliance programmes.
intro: This training programme equips supervisors and financial firms to apply the EU AI Act in financial services: classifying AI systems by risk, meeting provider and deployer obligations for high-risk credit and insurance uses, and integrating compliance with existing financial regulation.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give supervisors and practitioners a practical command of the AI Act as it applies to banks, insurers, investment firms and other financial entities, and of how it fits alongside financial services rules and data protection law. Participants leave able to classify AI use cases, assess compliance programmes and anticipate how financial supervisors will act as market surveillance authorities.
sections.What It Covers: The AI Act's risk-based approach and scope, prohibited practices and transparency duties, high-risk systems in credit and life and health insurance, provider and deployer obligations, fundamental rights impact assessments, general-purpose AI models, governance through the AI Office and national authorities, the role of financial supervisors, interplay with financial services rules and the GDPR, and the phased timeline and building a compliance programme.
Intended Audience: Supervisors, policy and innovation staff at national competent authorities responsible for AI used by financial entities
Compliance, risk, legal, data protection and model risk staff at banks, insurers, investment firms and payment firms
Senior managers and directors accountable for the firm's use of AI and its AI Act compliance
Learning Objectives: Explain the AI Act's risk-based approach, scope and key definitions as they apply to financial services
Identify prohibited practices and classify financial use cases, including creditworthiness and insurance pricing
Apply provider and deployer obligations, including risk management, data governance, human oversight and fundamental rights impact assessments
Explain the obligations for general-purpose AI models and the governance role of the AI Office
Assess how financial supervisors exercise market surveillance alongside financial services rules and data protection law
Design a proportionate AI Act compliance programme integrated with the firm's existing governance
sections.Structure and Format: Eight modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a multi-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a technical briefing with financial services case studies and classification exercises, and modules can be selected or tailored for supervisors or firms.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some familiarity with how AI or models are used in financial services is helpful. No technical or legal background is required.
Core Reading: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act)
Regulation (EU) 2016/679 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data (General Data Protection Regulation)
OECD, Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence (2019, revised 2024)
FSB, The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence (2024)

modules.title: The AI Act: Objectives, Scope and Risk-Based Approach
modules.summary: Why the EU legislated horizontally for AI, the definition of an AI system, material and territorial scope, the risk tiers, and how the Act borrows its architecture from EU product safety law.
objectives: Explain the AI Act's objectives and product-safety architecture
Apply the definition of an AI system and the main scope exclusions
Distinguish prohibited, high-risk, transparency-risk and minimal-risk systems
syllabus: Horizontal AI regulation, fundamental rights and the internal market
The AI system definition, Commission guidelines and traditional statistical models
Providers, deployers, importers, distributors and extraterritorial reach
The risk tiers and the AI literacy obligation

modules.title: Prohibited Practices and Transparency Obligations
modules.summary: The AI practices banned outright, those most relevant to financial services, and the transparency duties for chatbots, emotion recognition and AI-generated content used in customer journeys.
objectives: Identify prohibited practices and their relevance to financial services
Apply transparency obligations to customer-facing AI and synthetic content
Assess the controls that prevent prohibited uses within the firm
syllabus: Manipulative and exploitative techniques, social scoring and biometric categorisation
Emotion recognition in the workplace and its limited exceptions
Chatbot disclosure, deepfakes and labelling of AI-generated content
Red flags in marketing, collections and customer engagement tools

modules.title: High-Risk AI Systems in Financial Services
modules.summary: How AI systems are classified as high-risk, the financial use cases listed in Annex III, the filter for systems posing no significant risk, and how firms evidence and supervisors test classification decisions.
objectives: Apply the high-risk classification rules and the Annex III use cases
Classify creditworthiness, credit scoring and life and health insurance pricing systems
Document and challenge classification and derogation decisions
syllabus: Creditworthiness and credit scoring of individuals, and the fraud detection carve-out
Risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance
Employment, biometric and other Annex III uses within financial firms
Exercise: classifying a portfolio of financial AI use cases

modules.title: Obligations of Providers and Deployers
modules.summary: The requirements for high-risk systems, who carries them, when a financial firm becomes a provider by building or substantially modifying a system, and deployer duties including human oversight and fundamental rights impact assessments.
objectives: Apply requirements on risk management, data governance, documentation, accuracy and robustness
Determine when a firm is a provider, a deployer or both
Conduct a fundamental rights impact assessment for credit and insurance uses
syllabus: Risk management system, data governance, technical documentation and logging
Conformity assessment, registration and post-market monitoring
Deployer duties: human oversight, input data, monitoring and informing individuals
Fundamental rights impact assessments and the right to an explanation

modules.title: General-Purpose AI Models and the Value Chain
modules.summary: The obligations on providers of general-purpose AI models, including models with systemic risk, the role of the code of practice, and what financial firms building on such models need from providers.
objectives: Explain general-purpose AI model obligations and the systemic-risk classification
Assess the role of the code of practice and Commission guidelines
Manage dependency on general-purpose models through procurement, contracts and testing
syllabus: Technical documentation, copyright policy and training content summaries
Systemic-risk models: evaluation, serious incident reporting and cybersecurity
The general-purpose AI code of practice and Commission guidelines
Building on foundation models: value-chain information and DORA third-party risk

modules.title: Governance, the AI Office and Financial Supervisors
modules.summary: The AI Act's governance structure, from the AI Office and AI Board to national market surveillance authorities, and how financial supervisors take on market surveillance for regulated financial entities.
objectives: Explain the roles of the AI Office, the AI Board, the scientific panel and national authorities
Describe how financial supervisors act as market surveillance authorities for financial entities
Apply the enforcement and penalty framework proportionately
syllabus: The AI Office, AI Board, advisory forum and scientific panel
Financial supervisors as market surveillance authorities for regulated entities
Cooperation with data protection authorities, the ESAs and prudential supervisors
Investigations, corrective measures and administrative fines

modules.title: Interplay with Financial Services Rules and Data Protection
modules.summary: How AI Act obligations integrate with internal governance, model risk, consumer credit, insurance distribution and DORA requirements, and with the GDPR's rules on automated decision-making and impact assessments.
objectives: Map AI Act obligations onto existing financial services governance requirements
Apply the provisions that let financial firms meet obligations through internal governance rules
Align AI Act compliance with the GDPR, including automated decisions and DPIAs
syllabus: Quality management and monitoring through internal governance arrangements
Consumer credit, insurance distribution and conduct rules applied to AI
GDPR: lawful basis, automated decision-making and DPIAs alongside FRIAs
Model risk management, outsourcing and DORA as complementary frameworks

modules.title: Implementation Timeline and Building a Compliance Programme
modules.summary: The phased application of the AI Act, the dependence on standards, guidance and possible simplification adjustments, and how to build or supervise a proportionate compliance programme, ending with a planning workshop.
objectives: Explain the phased application of the Act and the role of harmonised standards
Design an AI inventory, classification process and compliance governance
Prepare a roadmap for the firm's or authority's AI Act implementation
syllabus: Phased application: prohibitions, general-purpose models, high-risk and product-embedded systems
Harmonised standards, guidance and proposed simplification adjustments
AI inventory, ownership, policies, AI literacy and assurance
Workshop: an AI Act implementation roadmap for the firm or authority

related.title: Digital Operational Resilience under DORA (EU Edition)
related.summary: An eight-module programme on DORA for supervisors and financial entities: ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing and TLPT, ICT third-party risk and critical provider oversight.

related.title: EU Payments Regulation: PSD2, PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation (EU Edition)
related.summary: An eight-module programme on EU payments regulation for supervisors and firms, covering PSD2 and EMD2 today and the PSD3 and Payment Services Regulation reform package.

related.title: Agentic Finance for Supervisors
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to understand and supervise AI agents that transact and make financial decisions, from agent identity to payments and liability.

related.title: AI Governance for Supervisors
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to assess firms' AI governance, model and fairness risk, and to shape the authority's approach to AI supervision.

related.title: EU Asset Management and Investment Fund Regulation (EU Edition)
related.summary: A ten-module programme mapping EU fund and asset management regulation, from UCITS, AIFMD and MiFID II to liquidity, delegation, cross-border marketing, SFDR and DORA.

related.title: MiCA Essentials for Supervisors (EU Edition)
related.summary: A six-module essentials programme giving EU national competent authority staff a practical command of MiCA, from token regimes and CASP authorisation to supervision and enforcement.
